text: Stranded. Ocean in every direction. A cup of it in your hand. Why can't you just drink the sea?
Free refills, you figure. Next to you sits a dented pot. So you take a sip. Big mistake.
Seawater is roughly 3.5 percent salt. Your blood is under 1 percent. You spit it out, in slow motion, like a sports replay.
Your kidneys can concentrate urine only a little beyond seawater's saltiness. And they also have to flush out your body's own waste.
Drinking seawater means you lose more water than you take in. Congratulations. You're thirstier.
Small sips won't save you. The sea is not a drink.
In 1943, a British lab tested seawater, mixed with fresh water, on a group of men.
Imagine you're one of them. By one account, the gain was small.
So how do people get fresh water when the sea won't do?
Take the Gulf. Hot, and short on rain: most of it gets around 120 millimeters a year, or less.
Early on, the answer was a boat. In the early 1900s, Kuwaiti boats carried fresh water from the Shatt al-Arab in Iraq.
Imagine you're the buyer on the dock, with one coin.
Imagine the jar leaks before it reaches you. You still pay for the full jar. Worst deal in history.
Oil made the money. Oil also powered the plants.
So how do you make the sea drinkable yourself? Two tricks.
Trick one: boil the sea, catch the steam, and leave the salt behind. It works. It also needs a lot of fuel.
Trick two. Squeeze seawater through a membrane that lets water through and blocks salt.
You try it with your cup. The pump wins, and you fly across the dock. Your tap sputters, then goes quiet.
By 2019, reverse osmosis was about half of Saudi Arabia's desalination capacity, per the IEA.
Boiling still ruled. In 2019, about two-thirds of the region's seawater output was thermal, meaning boiled.
By one 2026 analysis, desalination supplies about 99 percent of Qatar's drinking water.
Across the Middle East, desalination was only 3 percent of water in 2016. It took 5 percent of the region's energy.
So you pedal a bike wired to a pump. It stalls, and you fly over the handlebars.
Real plants run on fuel and power, not your legs.
Brine, the leftover, can harm the sea. Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Kuwait and Qatar make more than half the world's brine, by a 2019 study.
Then the sea fought back. In 2008 and 2009, a toxic algae bloom spread across the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Gulf.
The algae clogged intake filters. By one trade report, at least five UAE plants went offline.
Back at your tap, it coughs. Nothing comes out but gurgle.
In 1991, during the Gulf War, a black oil slick threatened to clog desalination intakes.
Crews rushed booms around the intakes. Estimates vary, but the spill was millions of barrels.
You get handed the end of the rope. It's the wrong end.
So can you drink the sea? Yes. But the sea fights back: it takes a very big plant and a lot of fuel.
Back on your rock, with the same cup and the same dented pot.
The lid catches the steam, and one drip lands on your forehead. The salt stays in the pot.
Many big plants do the same thing, just with a fuel bill.
Best deal you've had all week. Free refills, technically.
Subscribe for the next one. Just don't drink the sea.
